excerpts.text: HTTP semantics include the intentions defined by each request method ([Section 9](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#methods)), extensions to those semantics that might be described in request header fields, status codes that describe the response ([Section 15](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#status.codes)), and other control data and resource metadata that might be given in response fields.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-1.3-3)

For example, servers often scan portions of the User-Agent field value, and user agents often scan the Server field value, to adjust their own behavior with respect to known bugs or poorly chosen defaults.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-2.2-7)

A server that receives a request header field line, field value, or set of fields larger than it wishes to process MUST respond with an appropriate [4xx (Client Error)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#status.4xx) status code. Ignoring such header fields would increase the server's vulnerability to request smuggling attacks ([Section 11.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9112/#section-11.2) of [[HTTP/1.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#HTTP11)]).[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-5.4-2)
